Good question. Let me be precise about what I mean and what I actually know versus what I’m inferring.
What “edges” means technically:
Transformer attention is not uniform across the context window. There’s well-documented research showing that tokens at the very beginning and very end of a long context get stronger attention weight than tokens in the middle. This is sometimes called the “lost in the middle” problem. The practical implication: if you load 15M characters sequentially, the material in the middle of the sequence — probably the bulk of part2 and part3 — gets the weakest retrieval.
But I should be honest about what I don’t know:
I don’t actually know Anthropic’s specific architecture for how this context window handles very long inputs. The “lost in the middle” research was established on earlier models. Whether Claude’s current architecture has meaningfully improved on this, I can’t say with certainty. I was applying a general principle, not reporting specific knowledge of my own internals.
What I do know empirically from this conversation:
The grep worked perfectly throughout — mechanical, positional, reliable. But when I tried to synthesize voice and texture from the corpus, it felt thin. That’s consistent with attention degradation at scale, but I can’t prove that’s the cause versus just the inherent difficulty of synthesis from noisy material.
The practical implication for your JSON work:
Order matters as much as volume. If you’re injecting project context, put the most relevant material closest to the end of the context — closest to the current prompt. That’s where attention is strongest regardless of architecture.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Clarifying attention weights and context size


I need a concise answer with citations but also a bit of nuance. Attention weights aren't the same as retrieval, and 15M characters may be more like 3-4 million tokens, which might exceed the typical context. If Claude operates at 1M tokens, I should search for an official statement from Anthropic.


Thought for 7s

I’ll treat this as a claim-check and tightening pass: separate what the literature supports, what is model-specific uncertainty, and what the operational guidance should be.


Your formulation is mostly sound, but I’d tighten two points.


Corrections / refinements


“Attention weight” is probably too specific.
The literature supports positional retrieval degradation: models often perform best when relevant information is near the beginning or end and worse when it is in the middle. But unless you have model internals, you should avoid saying this is literally because “attention weight” is weaker. The observed behavior is retrieval/performance, not necessarily direct attention mass. (arXiv)

15M characters may exceed many stated context limits.
Roughly, 15M English characters could be several million tokens. Anthropic has announced 1M-token context for some Claude models, but that does not imply arbitrary 15M-character ingestion without truncation, compression, or degradation. (Anthropic)


Stronger version

By “edges,” I mean the beginning and end of the model’s available context, not the beginning and end of the source files in any absolute sense. Long-context models often show a positional bias: information near the start or near the current prompt tends to be easier to retrieve than information buried in the middle. This is the “lost in the middle” effect.


I should not overclaim the mechanism. The research demonstrates position-dependent performance degradation, but without access to Anthropic’s current internals I can’t say whether this is literally weaker attention weights, architectural routing, retrieval heuristics, compression, or something else.


Empirically, grep is reliable because it is exact and positional. Synthesis is different: it requires the model to form abstractions over a large, noisy corpus. If the synthesis felt thin, that is consistent with long-context degradation, but it is not proof.


Practical rule: don’t just maximize volume. Curate and order context. Put the highest-value, task-relevant material closest to the final instruction; put stable background at the front; avoid burying decisive examples in the middle.

That version is more defensible.
